title: The Warm or Cold Guest Lecturer
text:
In 1950 the psychologist Harold Kelley ran a simple study in classes at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Students were told that their regular instructor was away and that a guest would lead the session. Before he arrived, they were handed a short written note about him: his background, his teaching experience and a few traits.

Half the students got a note describing the guest as "a rather cold person, industrious, critical, practical, and determined." The other half got the same note with one change: "a very warm person." Then the guest came in and led a twenty-minute discussion, the same for everyone.

Afterward the students rated him. Those who had read "warm" saw him as more considerate, informal, sociable, popular, humorous and humane than those who had read "cold," although both groups had watched the same man doing the same things. The single word also changed behavior: Kelley noted that more of the students who expected a warm instructor took part in the discussion than of those who expected a cold one. One word in an introduction had shaped both the impression and the interaction that followed.
lesson: A single word said about someone before you meet can color everything you see. Be careful what labels you pass on, and hold the ones you receive lightly.
location: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, USA
source: Kelley, H. H. (1950). The warm-cold variable in first impressions of persons. Journal of Personality, 18(4), 431-439.
